questions.question_text: Find the volume of a sphere of radius $9$ cm, in exact form (in terms of $\pi$).

options.why: Squared the radius instead of cubing it ($r^{2}$ not $r^{3}$).

questions.question_text: A sphere has a diameter of $6$ cm. Find its volume in exact form (in terms of $\pi$).

options.why: Used the diameter $6$ as the radius instead of halving it to $3$.

questions.question_text: Find the volume of a sphere of radius $4$ cm, in cm³, correct to $1$ decimal place.

options.why: Squared the radius instead of cubing it ($r^{2}$ not $r^{3}$).

questions.question_text: A sphere has a volume of $288\pi$ cm³. Find its radius in cm.

options.why: Stopped at $r^{3} = 216$ and did not take the cube root.
Took the square root of $216$ instead of the cube root.

questions.question_text: The radius of a ball is tripled. How many times as large is the new ball’s volume?

options.why: Squared the scale factor ($3^{2}$) instead of cubing it.
Used the scale factor directly, without cubing it.

questions.solution_text:
$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$
Tripling the radius replaces $r$ with $3r$.
$V_{\text{new}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi (3r)^{3} = 27 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$
The new volume is $27$ times the original.

questions.question_text: A basketball is a sphere with a diameter of $24$ cm. Find its volume in cm³, to the nearest cubic centimetre.

options.why: Used the diameter $24$ as the radius instead of halving it to $12$.
Squared the radius instead of cubing it ($r^{2}$ not $r^{3}$).

questions.question_text: A sphere has a volume of $900$ cm³. Find its radius in cm, correct to $2$ decimal places.

options.why: Stopped at $r^{3} = 214.86$ without taking the cube root.
Divided by $4\pi$ instead of multiplying the volume by $\frac{3}{4\pi}$.

questions.question_text: A spherical balloon has a radius of $15$ cm. Find its volume in cm³, to the nearest cubic centimetre.
